name: GitHub
summary: Register an OAuth app or a GitHub App in a few minutes with no provider review. The real wait is org owners: new orgs block OAuth apps from org data until an owner approves.

paths.label: Your own repos
paths.detail: Solo developers and apps that act on personal repos.

paths.label: Organization repos
paths.detail: Your users connect repos owned by a company org.

links.label: Submit for Marketplace review
links.note: guide; you click Request publish on your listing page, OAuth apps can be listed

links.label: Ask in the Apps and API forum

verdicts.why: You fill in a short form in Developer settings and get a client ID right away, with no review by GitHub.
New organizations turn on OAuth app access restrictions by default, so your app cannot touch org data until an owner approves it.

skip.note: Composio offers managed OAuth for GitHub, so you can skip registering an app. GitHub's hosted MCP server sends clients to github.com/login/oauth, and that server's metadata has no registration_endpoint, so each MCP host must bring its own GitHub App or OAuth app.
whyOwnApp: You want a GitHub App with fine-grained permissions: Composio's GitHub App support is bring-your-own.
You want your own app name on the GitHub consent screen and in users' authorized apps list.
You want to control token expiry settings yourself.

requirements.label: A GitHub account or an org you administer
requirements.detail: You can create the app under your personal account or under any organization you administer.

requirements.label: Homepage URL
requirements.detail: The full URL of your app's website. Only put information in the app that you consider public.

requirements.label: Authorization callback URL
requirements.detail: Where GitHub sends users after they approve. The redirect_uri must match it exactly unless you turn on wildcard matching.

requirements.label: Choice of OAuth app or GitHub App
requirements.detail: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps for fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens. OAuth apps often need the broad repo scope.

requirements.label: Org owner approval
requirements.detail: For org-owned data, an org owner must approve your OAuth app, or install your GitHub App if it needs org permissions.

steps.title: Pick OAuth app or GitHub App
steps.detail: Read the comparison and pick one. Pick a GitHub App if you want fine-grained permissions instead of broad scopes.

steps.title: Register the app
steps.detail: Go to Settings, Developer settings, OAuth apps, New OAuth App. Enter the name, homepage URL and callback URL, then click Register application.

steps.title: Decide on expiring tokens
steps.detail: Expire user access tokens is on by default for new OAuth apps. Leave it on unless your code cannot refresh tokens yet.

steps.title: Store the client ID and secret
steps.detail: Copy the client ID and client secret from the app settings page into your secret store. The secret is needed to exchange codes for tokens.

steps.title: Write the web flow
steps.detail: Send users to /login/oauth/authorize with state and a PKCE S256 challenge, then exchange the code within 10 minutes at /login/oauth/access_token.

steps.title: Handle refresh tokens
steps.detail: Expiring access tokens last 8 hours and refresh tokens last 6 months without use. Code for both expiring and long-lived tokens.

steps.title: Test with your own account
steps.detail: Click Connect GitHub yourself and call the API with the token you get back.

steps.title: Get org owners to approve
steps.detail: Users can request owner approval for your OAuth app, and owners get a notification. Until then the app cannot reach private org resources.

scopes.name: repo
scopes.meaning: Full access to public and private repos, plus org-owned resources like projects, team memberships and webhooks.

scopes.name: read:org
scopes.meaning: Read-only access to org membership, org projects and team membership.

scopes.name: workflow
scopes.meaning: Add and update GitHub Actions workflow files.

scopes.name: offline_access
scopes.meaning: Ask for an expiring token plus a refresh token on one sign-in, even if the app does not force expiry.

limits.title: 100 OAuth apps per owner
limits.detail: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

limits.title: 10 callback URLs
limits.detail: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs per app.

limits.title: 10 tokens per user, app and scope
limits.detail: An 11th token for the same user and scopes revokes an older one. Creating more than 10 tokens in an hour triggers a re-authorization prompt instead.

limits.title: 5,000 requests per hour per user
limits.detail: OAuth tokens use the user's rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour. It is 15,000 when the app is owned or approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org.

limits.title: Codes expire in 10 minutes
limits.detail: Exchange the authorization code for a token within 10 minutes. Device codes last 15 minutes by default.

blockers.symptom: The token works but private org repos are missing or return errors.
blockers.fix: The org has OAuth app access restrictions on. Ask an org owner to approve your app, or switch to a GitHub App the owner installs.
Make it match a registered callback URL exactly. For local testing use 127.0.0.1 or ::1, where the port may differ.

blockers.symptom: Older tokens for a user stop working.
blockers.fix: You issued more than 10 tokens for the same user and scopes. Store and reuse one token per user instead of re-running the flow.

blockers.symptom: Some users have no refresh token.
blockers.fix: Turning on expiry does not change existing tokens, which stay long-lived. Handle both kinds, or ask those users to sign in again.
Turn on Enable Device Flow in the app settings first.
